He never asked. Tuners learn early that a piano is as often furniture for grief as an instrument. He simply lifted the lid, set his mutes, and worked while she sat in the kitchen with the door open, shelling beans or pretending to.

This year she was slower to answer the bell. She had a cane now, and the wax pears had been moved to make room for pill bottles.

"Same as always?" he asked.

"Same as always."

He worked through the temperament, then the bass, then up into the treble, where the strings were short and unforgiving. When he finished, he did what he always did. He played a few chords to check his work, then the little waltz he used as a test, sixteen bars, nothing special. His teacher had taught it to him.

In the kitchen, the shelling stopped.

It stopped every year, he realized. Every year, at exactly this point.

He turned on the bench. Through the doorway he could see her, hands still in the colander, eyes closed, face tipped up like someone feeling sun.

He had always thought she paid him for the tuning.

Tomas turned back to the keys. He played the sixteen bars again, and then, for the first time in eleven years, he kept going. He played the second strain, the repeat, the whole waltz, and after that another, and another, while the beans sat unshelled and the afternoon light moved across the floor.

When she paid him, it was the usual amount. He took it and said he'd come again in May.

Left at the Hendersons

My father taught me to drive in Greenlawn Cemetery because, he said, nobody there was in a hurry and nobody would be hurt if I hit them.

The car was his Corolla, a manual, with a clutch like a bad knee. On Sundays just after eight, when the gate was open but the mourners weren't up yet, we lurched down the gravel lanes at nine miles an hour.

He gave directions by headstone. "Left at the Hendersons. Straight on past the Okafor angel. Slow for the little lamb, there's a dip."

I thought it was a joke at first. By the third Sunday I noticed he wasn't reading the names. He knew where the Hendersons were before we could see them.

"How often do you come here?" I asked, and stalled.

"Clutch, then brake. Not the other way round."

"Dad."

"I walk here at lunch. It's quiet." He looked out his window. "Start her up again."

I started her up. We passed the angel and the lamb, and I waited for him to say the name I was expecting, down in the new section where the trees were still staked. He didn't. He said, "Reverse into that gap by the tap. Use your mirrors."

I did it badly, then less badly.

On the last Sunday before my test, he had me do a three-point turn at the bottom of the hill. The stone there was plain grey, with her name and two dates and nothing else, because we hadn't been able to agree on words. I got the car round in three without touching the verge.

"Good," he said. "She'd have told you to check your blind spot."

"She'd have told you to stop gripping the door."

He let go of the door. I brought the clutch up slowly, the way he'd shown me, and for once the car didn't jump. We rolled up the hill past the lamb and the angel, turned right at the Hendersons, and went out through the gate.

Middle C

The piano tuner arrived at ten, as he had every April for thirty-one years.

Mrs. Okafor let him in without a word. The house was quieter than he remembered. In the hall, a man's coat still hung on its hook, and a pair of reading glasses sat folded on the lid of the upright.

"He left those there," she said. "I haven't moved them."

Tomas set the glasses gently on the windowsill and opened the piano. Dust had settled on the hammers. No one had played it since autumn.

He worked the way he always did, string by string, listening for the wobble between two notes and easing it out until they became one. Mrs. Okafor sat in the armchair with tea going cold in her hands.

"I don't play," she said eventually. "I never did. I don't know why I called you."

"It drifts whether anyone plays it or not," Tomas said. "Weather. Time. The wood keeps moving."

"So it would just go on getting worse."

"Slowly. You wouldn't notice for a while. Then one day nothing would sound like itself."

She nodded as if he'd said something about more than pianos.

When he reached the high treble, he found a folded slip of paper wedged behind the last hammer. He handed it over without reading it. She opened it and laughed, a short, startled sound, like a key struck by accident.

"It's a shopping list," she said. "Eggs, stamps, lightbulbs. In his terrible handwriting." She pressed it flat against her knee. "Forty years of marriage, and that's what he hides in a piano."

"People put strange things in pianos."

He finished, closed the lid, and played a few bars to test it. The room filled up.

At the door she paid him, then hesitated.

"That note in the middle. The one you started with. Show me."

He came back in and pointed. She pressed it with one finger, held it down, and listened until the sound was entirely gone.

"Same time next April," she said.

The Last Tuning

By the time Oskar reached the Halloran house, half the valley had already been emptied. Doors stood open. A rocking chair sat in the road as if waiting for a bus.

Mrs. Halloran met him on the porch. "You'll think I'm foolish," she said.

"I think you're my eleven o'clock."

The piano was an upright Bechstein, too heavy for the moving trucks and too old to be worth the freight. In six weeks the dam gates would close, and the river would climb the hills until the church steeple was a rumor under forty feet of water. Everyone knew this. The piano was staying.

"I just can't leave it sour," she said.

Oskar opened the lid and set to work. He had tuned this instrument for thirty-one years: for her daughters' lessons, for two weddings, for one funeral where nobody played it at all. He knew its stubborn G, the way the bass strings sulked in wet weather. He took his time. He leaned on each pin until the wavering beats between strings slowed, slowed, and stilled.

When he finished, the afternoon had gone gold. Mrs. Halloran sat down and played a hymn, badly, the way she always had. Then she closed the fallboard and rested her hands on it.

"What do I owe you?"

"Nothing today."

She nodded, as if she had expected that, and pressed a jar of plum preserves on him anyway.

He drove out along the ridge road and stopped at the overlook. Below him lay the valley: the steeple, the orchards, the Halloran roof with its one missing shingle. He imagined the water coming, green and patient, filling the rooms. He imagined the piano standing in the dark, every string true, holding its pitch for a while down there. A month, maybe, before the rust.

A month of perfect silence, in tune.

He fished a plum from the jar with his fingers, ate it, and drove on.

What Was Owed

My father's hardware store closed on a Tuesday, three weeks after he died. I went in with a roll of trash bags and the intention to feel nothing.

Under the register, behind the spare receipt paper, I found a cigar box. Inside were slips of paper, hundreds of them, in his blocky handwriting. *Dale Meyers, 2 gal. exterior white, $38. Mrs. Okafor, sump pump, $112. Kid w/ bike, inner tube, $6.*

They were IOUs going back to 1987. None were crossed out.

I added them up on the back of an envelope. It took an hour. The total came to a little over forty thousand dollars. I thought of my mother clipping coupons at the kitchen table and my secondhand prom dress, and of the year we didn't fix the car. I had come to feel nothing, and now I was furious.

The bell above the door rang.

A man of about sixty stood there, cap in his hands. "Saw the light on," he said. "I'm Dale Meyers. Your dad…" He stopped and started again. "The winter the plant shut down, he let me have paint for my mother's house. Said pay when you can. Every time I tried, he told me the book was in the back and he was too busy to fetch it."

He laid two twenties on the counter.

"It was thirty-eight," I said.

"I know what it was."

After he left, I sat on the floor between the nail bins and the rope spools, holding the money. The store smelled of machine oil and sawdust, the way his shirts always had. I thought about Mrs. Okafor's dry basement and a kid riding home on two good tires.

I found a pencil stub and tore a corner from the envelope. *Dale Meyers,* I wrote. *Owed: $2.*

I put it in the box and the box back under the register.

Then I went home and left the light on.

Exact Change

On the last night of Booth 4, Marguerite brought a thermos and the good chair cushion, as if comfort mattered now.

The gantry was already up a quarter mile down the road, its cameras hooded in plastic like falcons. At six a.m. someone would pull the plastic off, and after that the cars would simply pass through, charged by a blink.

Nineteen years. She had worked it out once: something like two million hands. Hands with rings, hands with grease, a child's hand held up by a parent so he could pay the lady himself. She had been handed, over time, a warm pie, a kitten (declined), a phone number (declined, regretted), and once, at 3 a.m., a man's entire story about his brother, delivered in the time it took to break a twenty.

Tonight was thin. A milk tanker. A nurse who always had her quarters ready. A couple arguing so quietly it looked like prayer.

At 5:40 a pickup rolled in, and the driver, an old man in a feed-store cap, searched his ashtray, his pockets, the crack of the seat.

"I'm short thirty-five cents," he said. "I've been through here every Thursday since they built it. Never once short."

"It's all right."

"It isn't. I wanted to do it right. Last time and all."

So he knew. She hadn't expected anyone to know.

Marguerite took thirty-five cents from her own cardigan pocket, dropped it in the till, and raised the arm. "Paid in full."

He looked at her a while. Then he reached out the window and, having nothing else to give, shook her hand, the way you would at the end of a job done together.

His taillights shrank. Down the road, the wind had worked one corner of plastic loose from a camera, and it was flapping like something waving.

She waved back. Then she poured the last of the coffee and waited for six.

The Ladder

Three weeks after the funeral, Mr. Okafor appeared on Ruth's porch holding an aluminum ladder like a man carrying a confession.

"This is Dennis's," he said. "I borrowed it in 2003. For the gutters."

Ruth looked at it. It was paint-flecked, with one rubber foot missing and a strip of masking tape on the side rail that read HALVORSEN in her husband's blocky capitals.

"Twenty-one years," she said.

"I meant to bring it back. Then it had been a month, and it was embarrassing. Then a year, which was worse. After that I'd see him at the mailbox and we'd both just not mention it." He shifted his grip. "He did bring it up once. Said, 'Enjoying my ladder, Emeka?' I said yes, very much. He laughed, and that was the end of it."

Ruth could hear that laugh. That was the trouble with the house lately: everything in it had been finished. The crossword books, the half-jar of his mustard, the sweaters had all stopped being his and become merely left. She had spent three weeks closing accounts, and each phone call ended the same way, with a stranger telling her the matter was now settled.

And here was something unsettled. Something Dennis was still, in a sense, in the middle of.

"I can put it in the garage," Mr. Okafor offered.

"How are your gutters?"

He blinked. "Terrible, honestly. The maple."

"Then you're not done with it."

"Ruth, I can't—"

"He lent it to you. I don't recall him asking for it back." She touched the tape, the faded letters, then took her hand away. "Bring it home when you're finished, Emeka. No hurry."

He stood a moment, eyes bright, then nodded and turned the ladder carefully around on the narrow porch. She watched him carry it back across the lawn, the label catching the light. It was her husband's name, still out in the world, still owed.

The Tuner

Every April, Mrs. Adeyemi called Tomas to tune a piano nobody played.

It was an upright Bechstein in walnut, wedged between a window and a bookcase. Her husband had played it. He had been dead eleven years, and for eleven years Tomas had come with his leather roll of tools, lifted the lid, and coaxed two hundred and thirty strings back toward agreement.

"It drifts," she always said, setting tea on the windowsill. "Even when no one touches it."

"Especially then," he always answered.

This year he worked more slowly. The high notes had been leaving him since autumn, first the top octave, then the one beneath, a quiet tide going out. He leaned his ear close to the strings and heard mostly the memory of what they should be. He tuned by the feel of the lever in his palm, by the beats trembling through the wood into his wrist.

When he finished, he closed the lid and did not look at her.

"Mrs. Adeyemi, I should recommend someone else for next year. Someone younger."

She was quiet. Then she crossed the room, sat on the bench, and lifted the fallboard. He had never seen her touch the keys.

She played a scale, slowly, with one finger, all the way to the top. Then came a few bars of something, a hymn perhaps, clumsy and bare.

"It's right," she said. "Every note."

"You play."

"Badly. Every night since he died." She smiled at the keys. "I let you believe otherwise. I thought a silent piano would seem sadder, and you'd keep coming."

Tomas laughed, surprising himself.

"Next April," she said, "you'll tune by hand, and I'll sit here and tell you when it's true. Between your wrist and my ears, we make one decent tuner."

He picked up his tea. It had gone cold, as it did every year. He drank it anyway, and asked her to play the hymn again.

Exact Change

On the last night of the Route 9 toll plaza, Dolores counted her drawer twice out of habit, though nobody would audit it. By morning the gantry overhead would read license plates on its own, and booth four would be a box of glass waiting for a crane.

Traffic thinned after midnight the way it always did. A trucker hauling onions. Two teenagers who paid in nickels and apologized. A nurse in scrubs who never looked up.

At 4:10 the bakery van arrived, right on time for nineteen years.

"Dollar seventy-five," Dolores said.

"Highway robbery," said Marcus, and handed over the coins, warm from his palm, along with a paper bag. Tonight the bag was heavier than usual.

"That's not a roll."

"It's a whole loaf. Retirement gift." He drummed the steering wheel. "What'll you do now?"

"Sleep at night, apparently. I hear people recommend it."

"Overrated. Nothing's open." He hesitated. Behind him the road was empty, no headlights, no one to hold up. In nineteen years he had never once stayed longer than a green light allowed. "Shop opens at six. Coffee's bad, but the bread's honest. We're on Alder Street, if you ever wondered where I was going."

She had wondered. She'd pictured it a hundred ways: brick, a blue awning, flour on the windows.

"Is there an awning?"

"Green. Faded."

"Close," she said.

He laughed, not understanding, and the van pulled forward under the new cameras, which blinked and recorded his plate and knew nothing else about him.

At six, Dolores hung her vest on the hook, left the drawer balanced to the penny, and raised the gate arm by hand one final time, for no one. Then she drove east with a loaf on the passenger seat, toward Alder Street, paying nothing, feeling for the first time what it was like to pass through.

**The Last Crossing**

Tomorrow the bridge would open, and nobody would need Anselm or his ferry again.

He made the morning run as he had for thirty-one years: six cars, a bread van, the Okafor twins with their bicycles. The river was the colour of weak tea. Upstream, the new bridge stood with ribbons already tied to its railings, waiting to be cut.

Mrs. Varga boarded at noon, on foot, as she did every Thursday. She paid her two coins, stood at the rail for the crossing, and did not get off on the other side. She never did. She rode back, thanked him, and walked home.

In thirty-one years he had never asked. Today, mid-river, he cut the engine.

"The bridge," he said. "You'll be able to walk across. Anytime you like."

"I don't want to get across." She kept her eyes on the water. "My father ran this boat before you. Did you know? He let me steer right about here, where the current pulls left. I was seven. He'd stand behind me and pretend he wasn't holding the wheel."

The ferry drifted. A heron lifted from the reeds.

"It's the only place I can still feel his hands," she said.

Anselm looked at the wheel, worn pale in two places by palms older than his. He'd always assumed he'd done that himself.

He stepped aside.

Mrs. Varga was eighty-three, and she crossed the deck slowly, the way people walk in church. She set her hands exactly on the pale places. He restarted the engine and stood behind her with his own hands in his pockets.

The current pulled left. She corrected for it without thinking.

"They're selling her for scrap," he said, as the far bank neared. "I thought I might make an offer."

"What would you do with a ferry and no one to carry?"

"Thursdays," Anselm said. "I'd have Thursdays."

She laughed, and brought them in crooked, and he let her.

The Lighthouse Keeper's Last Letter

Marta had kept the light on Harrow Point for thirty-one years, and in all that time she had never once missed a dusk.

The automation crew arrived on a Tuesday. Two young men with a crate of sensors and a tablet, polite and efficient, finished by noon. "It'll run itself now," the taller one said. "You can finally sleep through the night."

She thanked them and made tea she didn't drink.

That evening she climbed the ninety-two steps anyway. The new lamp clicked on by itself, precisely at sunset, steady and indifferent. She stood beside it with her hands in her pockets, feeling like a guest in her own house.

Below, the sea went about its business. A trawler slid past the rocks, heading home. Its captain, old Petrakis, gave three short blasts of the horn, as he had every evening for two decades. Marta reached for the brass signal lever out of habit, then stopped. The crew had disconnected it.

She thought for a moment. Then she took the lantern from its hook by the stairs, lit it, and swung it three times in the window.

A pause. Then one long blast from the trawler, low and warm across the water.

Marta smiled. She sat at the little desk where she had filled in logbooks for three decades and began a letter to the harbor board. She wrote that the new system worked beautifully. She wrote that she would be leaving the cottage by spring, as agreed.

Then she crossed out the last line.

"I will stay on," she wrote instead, "at no cost to the board. The lamp can guide the ships. But someone ought to answer them."

She sealed the envelope, set it by the door, and climbed back up to watch the dark come in.

The Lighthouse Keeper's Last Letter

Every evening for forty years, Tomas climbed the one hundred and twelve steps to light the lamp. Tonight his knees ached with each one, and he counted them aloud as if saying goodbye.

The automated system would arrive tomorrow. A man from the mainland had explained it kindly, with pamphlets. No more keeper needed. A sensor would know when darkness fell.

At the top, Tomas sat beside the great lens and took out paper and pen.

*To whoever comes after,* he wrote, then stopped. No one would come after. That was the point.

He started again.

*To the lamp,*

*You'll think me foolish. But I have spoken to you more than to any living soul, so it seems right.*

*I was twenty-three when I came here, running from a grief I won't name. I thought the solitude would bury me. Instead, you gave me a purpose simple enough to hold: when dark comes, make light.*

*I never met the sailors we guided home. But some nights I'd watch a ship's lantern slide safely past the rocks, and I'd think, there go fathers. There go daughters. There goes someone's whole world, and they'll never know my name.*

*That was enough. It turns out that was plenty.*

*The machine won't love you. But it will keep you burning, and maybe that's the same thing in the end.*

He folded the letter and tucked it behind the brass housing, where no technician would think to look.

Then he lit the lamp by hand, one last time. The beam swept out across the black water, steady and sure.

Far out, a small fishing boat turned toward harbor.

Tomas watched until it was safe. Then he went down the stairs, counting backward, smiling at every step.

The Lighthouse Keeper's Last Letter

Marta had tended the lamp at Gull Point for forty-one years, and in all that time she had never missed a night. So when the letter came announcing that the light would be automated by spring, she read it twice, folded it carefully, and used it to level the wobbly leg of her kitchen table.

Winter passed the way it always did. Storms came in sideways off the water. She climbed the ninety-two steps each dusk, trimmed what needed trimming, polished the great lens until it held her reflection like a patient eye.

In March, a young technician named Dev arrived with crates of equipment. He was apologetic about it, which she appreciated.

"It's a good system," he said, wiring a small gray box to the wall. "Never sleeps."

"Neither did I," Marta said, and made him tea.

He worked for three days. On the last evening, he showed her the switch that would hand everything over to the machine. "You can do the honors, if you want."

She looked at it for a long moment. Then she shook her head. "Come up with me first."

They climbed together. At the top, the sea spread out in every direction, bruised purple under the fading sky. A single fishing boat was working its way home, small as a thumbnail.

"That's Aldo's boy," she said. "His father came in by this light, and his grandfather too. Your box doesn't know that."

Dev was quiet. "No," he admitted. "It doesn't."

"Then you'll have to know it for a while." She pressed a worn brass key into his hand, the one for the lamp room door. "Somebody should."

She lit the lamp herself one final time. The beam swept out across the darkening water, and far below, the little boat turned toward it and came steadily home.

The Lighthouse Keeper's Last Letter

Marta had kept the light on Corran Rock for thirty-one years, and in all that time she had never missed a night. So when the letter came saying the lamp would be automated in spring, she read it twice, folded it into her apron pocket, and went up the stairs to trim the wick as usual.

The winter passed slowly. She polished the brass until it showed her face. She oiled the gears, scrubbed the salt from the windows, and wrote in the logbook each evening: Light lit. Sea calm. Or: Light lit. Gale from the northwest.

In March, a young engineer arrived with crates of equipment. He was polite and embarrassed, and he kept apologizing as he bolted the new mechanism into place.

"It will run by itself," he said. "You won't have to climb those stairs anymore."

"I liked the stairs," Marta said.

On her final night, a fog rolled in thick as wool. The new lamp turned steadily, obediently, needing nothing. Marta sat beside it anyway, her hands idle in her lap.

Near midnight she heard it: a small engine, sputtering, somewhere too close to the rocks. The beam swept over the fog and showed nothing. A light could warn, but it could not listen.

Marta ran down the hundred and twelve steps, seized the old brass hand bell from its hook, and rang it from the landing until her arm burned. She rang it into the blind white dark, steady as a heartbeat.

The engine turned. Faded. Found the channel.

In the morning, a fisherman's boy rowed out with a basket of bread and a note from his father: Heard you. Thank you.

Marta opened the logbook and wrote her last entry.

Light lit. Fog heavy. Bell rung.

Then she left the bell on the engineer's desk, where he would find it.

The Clockmaker's Last Repair

Old Tomas had fixed every clock in the village for fifty years, but the one on his own mantel had been silent since the winter his wife died.

He told people he was too busy. There was always a pocket watch with a cracked crystal, a cuckoo that sang at the wrong hour, a church tower whose hands drifted in the wind. His neighbors nodded and did not press him.

One gray afternoon, a girl of about nine came into the shop carrying a shoebox. Inside lay a small brass alarm clock in a dozen pieces.

"I took it apart to see where the ticking lived," she said. "Now I can't find it."

Tomas laughed for the first time in months. He cleared a space on the bench and pulled up a second stool.

"The ticking doesn't live in any one part," he said. "It lives in how they meet."

They worked until the windows went dark. He showed her the mainspring, the escapement, the tiny wheel that rocked back and forth like a heartbeat. Her fingers were clumsy but patient. When the last screw turned, she wound the key and held the clock to her ear.

Her whole face opened.

After she left, the shop felt larger than usual. Tomas stood a long while in front of the mantel. Then he lifted the silent clock down, carried it to the bench, and opened its back.

Nothing was broken. It had only wanted winding. Anna had done it every Sunday evening, humming, and he had never once thought to do it himself.

He turned the key slowly, eight times, the way she used to.

The ticking filled the room, steady and unhurried, as though it had simply been waiting for him to listen.

Tomas put the kettle on and set out two cups from habit. This time, he left them both.

The Lighthouse Keeper's Last Letter

Maren had kept the light for forty-one years, and in all that time she had never once seen the ship she was waiting for.

Her father had told her about it when she was small: a blue-hulled schooner called the *Wren*, lost in fog the night she was born. "Ships come back," he'd said, trimming the wick. "Sometimes it just takes them a while."
